subject: Materials Science
title: Biodegradation: Nature's Recycling
description: A quick, practical guide to Biodegradation: Nature's Recycling.

hook.text: A PLA cup in a compost pile disappears in six months. A polystyrene cup in a landfill lasts centuries.

buildup.text: Biodegradable polymers have bonds that microorganisms can break — ester, amide, or glycosidic linkages.

discovery.text: Enzymes from bacteria and fungi cleave the polymer chains into small molecules — CO₂, water, and biomass.

twist.text: Most 'biodegradable' plastics only degrade in industrial composters at 60°C — not in oceans or landfills.

climax.text: PHA plastics made by bacteria are truly biodegradable in soil and sea — but cost five times more than polyethylene.

punchline.text: Biodegradation is nature's solution — if we design the polymer to cooperate.

quiz.question: Why don't most 'biodegradable' plastics break down in oceans?
options: They require industrial composting temperatures around 60°C to degrade
